descriptions.Fairness: The capacity to weigh competing interests, make equitable judgements, and cooperate constructively with others.
descriptions.Empathy: The capacity to understand and connect with others’ perspectives and lived experience.
descriptions.Discernment: The capacity to critically examine details, distinguish what is relevant, and identify meaningful distinctions.
descriptions.Objectivity: The capacity to evaluate claims against evidence, minimise bias and assumptions, and generate independent insights.
descriptions.Tenacity: The capacity to persist through obstacles, sustain effort, and remain committed to achieving goals.
descriptions.Courage: The capacity to proactively initiate and act on self-directed, purposeful decisions, undaunted by uncertainty or risk.
descriptions.Confidence: The capacity to believe in one’s own abilities and judgement, enabling self-assured action.
descriptions.Prudence: The capacity to act with care and restraint, applying cautious judgement to avoid unnecessary risk.
descriptions.Foresight: The capacity to reflect on current conditions, project future outcomes, and pre-emptively adapt to change.
descriptions.Practicality: The capacity to respond to real-world constraints with grounded composure and apply effective, workable solutions.
descriptions.Curiosity: The capacity to seek out new information, explore ideas, deepen understanding, and communicate findings.
descriptions.Discipline: The capacity to consistently execute planned actions and meet obligations, reliably and responsibly.

Curiosity.description: A tendency to seek out and acquire new work-related knowledge and obtain a deep understanding of work-related subjects.

Discernment.description: A tendency to be detail-oriented, organised, and thorough in completing work.

Discipline.label: Dependability
Discipline.description: A tendency to be reliable, responsible, and consistent in meeting work-related obligations.

Empathy.label: Empathy
Empathy.description: A tendency to show concern for others and be sensitive to others' needs and feelings at work.

Fairness.label: Cooperation
Fairness.description: A tendency to be pleasant, helpful, and willing to assist others at work.

Foresight.label: Adaptability
Foresight.description: A tendency to be open to and comfortable with change, new experiences, or ideas at work.

Objectivity.label: Innovative
Objectivity.description: A tendency to be inventive, to be imaginative, and to adopt new perspectives on ways to accomplish work.

Practicality.label: Self-Control
Practicality.description: A tendency to remain calm and composed and to manage emotions effectively in response to criticism or difficult situations at work.

Prudence.label: Cautiousness
Prudence.description: A tendency to be careful, deliberate, and risk-avoidant when making work-related decisions or doing work.

Tenacity.label: Perseverance
Tenacity.description: A tendency to exhibit determination and resolve to perform or complete tasks in the face of difficult circumstances or obstacles at work.

overview:
About This Report

This report provides an overview of your SSM Assessment® strengths profile and how it may relate to patterns of communication, collaboration, and overall team dynamics at work. It is designed to support self-awareness, reflection, and developmental discussion in team and workshop settings.

The SSM Assessment measures personality — how you tend to behave — rather than abilities or skills (what you are good at) or interests (what you enjoy doing). It is not intended to provide any clinical diagnosis.

The Assessment is grounded in established personality research and has completed phase one psychometric validation. Report insights should still be interpreted as indicative tendencies rather than definitive predictive measures, and the tool is not intended for hiring, promotion, or related HR decisions.

In this report, your SSM Assessment profile is also conceptually aligned to O*NET Work Styles and Work Activities.

The O*NET Resource Center is a professional workforce research portal providing data, tools, technical documentation, and support. It is widely recognised as a global standard in workplace metrics.

howToReadMatrix:
How to Read This Chart

The Shaw Strengths Matrix (SSM) synthesises four interrelated frameworks into one, providing nuanced insights into your unique preference rankings. It integrates how we:

• Apply our Cognitive Preferences — Intuition, Thinking, Feeling, and Sensing
• Express these across our Temporal Preferences — Past Reflection, Present Engagement, and Future Anticipation
• Intersects these into 12 character strengths, uniquely ranked per individual into 479 million possible combinations.

Each Strength is therefore a composite of both Cognitive Preference and Temporal Preference.

SSM defines character strengths as "Stable, positive traits expressed in our behaviour that contribute to wellbeing and flourishing. While their expression varies across situations, our overall strength profile remains relatively stable over time."

Your survey responses were scored and ranked using a standardised algorithm designed to ensure consistent comparison across all Strengths.

These rankings reflect patterns described in the CAPS model (Mischel & Shoda). Your higher-ranked Strengths are those more readily accessible to you and therefore guide your responses in real-world situations more often.
howToReadAssessmentTable:
How to Read This Chart

The SSM Assessment Table presents a high-level summary of the results from your completed assessment.
It ranks the measured presence of the 12 SSM strengths in your personality — based on your responses to workplace scenario questions — from 1 (strongest) to 12 (least expressed).

Your strengths are grouped into four categories:

a) Signature Strengths (#1-#3) – core strengths you naturally and consistently use—your go-to abilities that define how you operate in flow and at your best.
b) Supporting Strengths (#4-#6) – readily accessible strengths that reinforce your core abilities—dependable when needed, but not primary.
c) Stretch Strengths (#7-#9) – strengths you deploy which are effective when needed, but requiring more focus and effort than the first two categories.
d) Situational Strengths (#10-#12) – lesser used strengths that emerge only in specific situations, and are energy-intensive to deploy over longer periods.
howToReadWorkStyles:
How to Read This Chart

This chart maps your 12 ranked SSM strengths to the 12 core O*NET Work Styles, illustrating how your strengths translate into observable workplace behaviours.

Your SSM Assessment rankings (1–12) and Categories (Signature, Supporting, Stretch, and Situational) align directly with the closest matched O*NET Work Styles listed here.

O*NET defines Work Styles as "personal characteristics that can affect how well someone performs a job."
They represent the workplace expression of your strengths — showing how your inner traits are activated and applied in professional settings.

Your Work Styles ranking reveals the underlying "why" — your motivation and natural approach to work.
howToReadWorkActivities:
How to Read This Chart

This chart shows your 12 ranked SSM strengths alongside the O*NET Work Activities most strongly aligned with each strength, illustrating how your strengths may be expressed through different types of work tasks.

Note, the Work Activity alignments reflect ShawSight's LLM-based interpretation of O*NET Work Activity data, identifying the Work Activities with the strongest alignment to each SSM strength.
Your SSM Assessment rankings (1–12) and Categories are shown alongside the corresponding O*NET Work Activities.

O*NET defines Work Activities as "general types of job behaviours occurring on multiple jobs."
They represent the task-level expression of your strengths.

Your Work Activities describe the "how" — the types of tasks and activities through which your strengths are most likely to be expressed.
